slides.title: Africa's designated driver network.

slides.headline: Africa is the worst place in the world to drink and drive.

stats.label: of road deaths involve alcohol — nearly 3× the global average of 20%
annual economic cost of alcohol-related crashes
road deaths per 100,000 people — among Africa's worst, weak DUI enforcement, no scalable alternative

status_quo.label: What people do instead
status_quo.workaround: Two separate Bolt rides — one home, one back to retrieve the car in the morning.
status_quo.note: Keys is price-competitive with the workaround, and removes the morning retrieval entirely.

compound_insights: The morning car retrieval is worse than the night ride — it's the more painful, underserved half of the problem.
People drive impaired because they don't trust an unknown Bolt driver with their keys — it's an identity trust problem, not a laziness problem.
Nobody plans to drink and drive. The decision happens in the car park at 1am when everyone else is leaving.
slides.insight: And yet — no scaled, app-based designated-driver category exists anywhere on the continent.

slides.headline: We've lived this problem. Here's what we've observed.

archetype.label: Day-1 customer
archetype.description: Owns a vehicle worth ₦8M–25M. Active in Victoria Island and Lekki nightlife 2–4 nights per month. Has tried the two-Bolt workaround. Trusts a vetted, named driver — not an anonymous platform stranger — to handle their keys.
archetype.why: Owns the car. Cares about it. Has social capital to refer 3+ people after a single good experience. Present at the exact venues and hours where demand concentrates.

observations.label: The retrieval problem is worse than the night ride
observations.body: Getting home is solved. Getting your car back at 9am from a venue 12 km away — with no breakfast, no ride, and a work call at 10 — is the part nobody talks about.

observations.label: Trust blocks more decisions than price
observations.body: Handing a ₦15M SUV to an anonymous driver feels riskier than driving impaired. The barrier isn't cost awareness — it's identity verification at the moment of key handoff.

observations.label: The decision happens at 1am in a car park
observations.body: Nobody plans to drink and drive. The decision is made when everyone else is leaving and there's no pre-booked alternative. Booking at 8pm (or a venue QR at the door) is the only intervention that works.

slides.headline: This isn't a thesis. China has been running it for a decade.

model.name: Daijia
model.how_it_works: A driver arrives at your location on a foldable e-bike, stows it in your trunk, and drives you home in your own car. You pay through the app.
model.why_it_works: Zero fleet cost. The user keeps their car. The driver pool is decoupled from vehicle ownership. Unit economics survive in markets where labor is cheap relative to private vehicle cost.

slides.headline: Why a dozen Western attempts have stalled.

failures.name: BeMyDD
failures.note: US designated-driver app, ~2010s. Failed to reach unit economics in suburban markets — driver dispatch cost exceeded rider willingness to pay.

failures.name: Dryver
failures.note: Still operating in select US cities, but stayed regional. Could not break out of franchise model.

failures.name: STEER
failures.note: App-based DD service. Quiet exit; could not solve insurance liability at scale.

failures.name: Designated Driver Inc. → To Arrive Alive (Canada)
failures.note: Acquired in 2022. Consolidation play, not a growth story.

slides.pattern: Three structural blockers in Western markets: (1) labor cost makes the human-driven-home model uneconomic vs Uber Black; (2) insurance liability for a non-owner driving an impaired customer's car is unsolved; (3) demand density never reaches the dispatch threshold. None of these apply with the same force in the African markets we target.

slides.headline: Why Africa works where the West didn't.

reasons.title: Labor economics flip the model
reasons.body: A Bolt driver in Lagos earns ~₦8,000–15,000/day. A premium per-trip rate of ₦12,000–20,000 for a 45-minute drive-home job pulls supply without subsidies — impossible math in London or LA.

reasons.title: Concentrated nightlife corridors
reasons.body: Victoria Island + Lekki (Lagos), Sandton + Rosebank (JoBurg), Westlands + Kilimani (Nairobi). Dense demand within 5–8 km radii — exactly the geography daijia needs.

reasons.title: Enforcement is rising, fast
reasons.body: FRSC ramping DUI checkpoints. SA's National Road Traffic Amendment Act lowered BAC to 0.00. Government tailwind without government dependency.

reasons.title: Bolt is already there
reasons.body: 60%+ market share in Nigeria. Leader in 5 African markets. $104M committed to Africa safety initiatives over 3 years (Nov 2024). The distribution rail is built.

slides.market: Africa's ride-hailing market: USD 2.85B (2024) → USD 4.28B by 2032. Designated driving is the missing premium category in that growth.

steps.title: Request
steps.body: User opens Bolt. Taps 'Keys' category (new tab next to Economy / Comfort).

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Certified Keys driver dispatched on foldable e-bike. ETA shown live.

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: Driver arrives. Pre-ride 360° vehicle scan via app for damage protection.

steps.title: Drive
steps.body: E-bike folds into trunk. Driver takes user home in user's own car.

steps.title: Settle
steps.body: Drop-off, photo confirmation, payment via Bolt wallet. Driver e-bikes back out.

slides.headline: Three structural advantages Bolt cannot replicate.
slides.intro: A fast follower can clone the app in 90 days. They cannot clone what the app builds over 24 months.

moat_layers.title: Identity Graph
moat_layers.body: Every completed trip adds a data point: which driver handled which keys, at what hour, at which venue, with what outcome. After 10,000 trips, you own the only verified driver-trust dataset in African nightlife. Bolt has ride ratings. You have key-handoff history. Those are different assets — and yours transfers directly to insurance underwriting.
moat_layers.bolt_cannot: Bolt rates drivers on ride quality, not key custody. Retraining the data model requires starting over.

moat_layers.title: Venue Distribution
moat_layers.body: Once 50 clubs and hotels in Lagos put a Keys QR at the exit, you own the moment of demand. Bolt would need to negotiate the same 50 deals — and agree not to compete on standard rides (they won't). You offer venues a 5% referral commission per booking; Bolt's margin structure makes that structurally awkward.
moat_layers.bolt_cannot: Bolt's incentives misalign with venue exclusivity. A venue partner who sends rides to Keys is also sending rides away from standard Bolt Economy.

moat_layers.title: Liability Framework
moat_layers.body: A licensed 'car custody' operator carries per-trip third-party-driver insurance that Bolt's ToS explicitly excludes. When FRSC formalises DUI checkpoints (it's coming), Keys is the compliant option. Bolt becomes the liability.
moat_layers.bolt_cannot: Bolt's legal team will not accept liability for a non-Bolt vehicle driven by a third party. That constraint is structural, not fixable with a product update.

slides.flywheel: Trust data → insurance credibility → venue partnerships → more trip data → better matching → deeper trust data.
slides.moat_statement: The flywheel compounds. Each layer makes the next harder to replicate — and the data advantage widens every week you operate.

strategic_fit.title: Defends premium segment
strategic_fit.body: Uber's Africa play has been a steady push into Comfort/XL/EV. Keys gives Bolt a category Uber can't match without 12+ months of build.

strategic_fit.title: Activates the $104M safety mandate
strategic_fit.body: Bolt's own commitment makes this strategically pre-approved. Keys is the most concrete way to demonstrate DUI reduction in market.

strategic_fit.title: Unlocks the alcohol industry as a partner
strategic_fit.body: Diageo, Pernod Ricard, Heineken all run DUI-prevention CSR budgets in Africa. Keys is the channel they've been waiting for.

strategic_fit.title: Locks in higher-LTV riders
strategic_fit.body: Car owners using designated driving are upper-middle-class repeat customers — exactly the cohort Bolt is competing for.

slides.headline: From Lagos to the Gulf in 24 months.

phases.title: Lagos Pilot
phases.detail: VI + Lekki + Ikoyi only. 50 trained drivers. Underwriter agreement signed. 8 launch venue partners (Quilox, Hard Rock, RSVP, etc.). Target: 2,000 completed trips, sub-2% incident rate.

phases.title: Lagos Scale + Johannesburg
phases.detail: Lagos to 200+ drivers. Sandton/Rosebank launch, partnering with Bolt SA. SA insurance product (RTMC-aligned). 12,000 cumulative trips.

phases.title: Nairobi + Cape Town
phases.detail: Westlands launch. Cape Town V&A corridor. Multi-country ops playbook locked. First alcohol-brand sponsorship contract (Diageo / Pernod Ricard).

phases.title: Gulf Expansion
phases.detail: Dubai pilot — exact unit economics fit (cheap labor + expensive cars + strict DUI). Bolt entered Dubai Dec 2024; Keys becomes the safety-led differentiator vs Careem.
